hypothesis: Host and native models reproduce the queue's lifecycle, sharing, recovery, VM and ring behavior.
narrative: Lifecycle evidence under ~/.cache/sunstoneos/build/gpu-integrate-1031/lifecycle/: fourteen queue cases, ten public open/close cycles, two admitted callers, preserved peer jobs through timeout and reset, serial exhaustion and failed-isolation retention. The actual native backend passes eleven reset-policy scenarios, and the stop sanitizer check covers 123 retained failures. Native quiescence checks cover returning and resident images, including late peer admission, unchanged close deadlines and the actual recovery-limit producer. The native peer fixture executes application admission, real static queue construction and submission through the OS readiness hook; device effects and scheduling remain modeled. The three baseline builds and recorded QEMU recognition pass. Mimus shader, program, readout, placement and qualification-mode checks pass; the compiled shader occupies 7,576 bytes and uses 107 temporary registers. The frozen recognition image enables exhaustive sum comparison. Three lifecycle reviewers (simplicity, hardware behavior, correctness) approved. Review corrections cover zero-job shutdown and cold return, SLC bypass for CPU/GPU-shared mappings, rounded lease isolation, program-source bounds and application-supplied startup initialization (review-fixes/ in the cache directory); returning images also produce an untouched receipt when GPU construction was skipped, run in hello-compute and mimus images (review-followup/). Original single-caller host queue model: 38 service cases and an external 204-job replay with 5,870,398 checked sums. Native instruction models: 16 thermal cases, 10 public-client cases, 18 returning-image cases and 71 constructor-refusal and cold-return cases. Output-permission checks cover two applications. The VM check covers four admitted page sizes and 36 refusals and compares tables with the pinned driver. The ring trace records 23 aligned stores per job, plus five stores when a padding record wraps the ring; no buffer data is copied. Raw commands, input snapshots, image hashes and results: ~/.cache/sunstoneos/build/gpu-queue-1031/ (checks/ queue and native fixtures; program/ compiler and vector checks; mimus-client/ application arithmetic and recorded-recognition evidence). Sizes: the shared-client queue occupies 2,632 bytes on AArch64 including a 360-byte peer slot and completion queue, plus a fixed 16 KiB peer task stack in GPU images; the original single-client queue occupied 2,240 bytes; device allocations are 79 write-back pages (34 firmware, 21 payload, 24 table) and 51 uncached pages for the mimus layout. The frozen packages retained a CPU clock failure while lowering CPU-B to 1014 MHz during return (CPU-return stage 0x0204 retains each clock phase and driver state); the separate CPU clock worker owned the correction and the packages were refrozen. The frozen recognition run and lifecycle packages were requested through the coordinator; the runner uses tools/dev-run.py and captures the image-bound GPU receipt and thermal window before restoring RAM.

hypothesis: The queue's per-job CPU cost exceeds the earlier mimus session's by at most 0.5 µs on an A76.
prediction: The host model counted these operations per job of the earlier mimus session: 1 worker step to the kick, 57 transport and 6 maintenance DSB SY, 6 queue operations, 25 critical sections and 27 translations in the backend's register callbacks. The queue keeps the transport, kernel command queue, backend and interrupt path, so those counts stay. Differences per job: job description copies 160 bytes twice instead of 24 bytes twice (about 70 more 8-byte loads and stores); admission about 25 compares instead of at most 13 (about 12 more); PDS data 2 compares per job; argument block and CDM stream 32 and 60 bytes, unchanged; job-page clean 2 lines, unchanged; client-ring writes 23 aligned 8-byte stores, unchanged (replacing the session's 184 single-byte stores, 161 fewer uncached stores); completion one timeline load and one record. The estimate uses one cycle per load, store or compare, about 85 cycles per job; allowing four times that for cache misses and mispredicted branches gives at most 400 cycles: 0.2 µs on an A76 at 2,002 MHz and 0.8 µs on an A55 at 494 MHz, at most 0.25% of the smallest measured job time on an A76 and 1% on an A55 (job times 80 to 83 µs kick-to-timeline, 87 µs after the ring wrap, 113 µs after an MMU cache flush). Creation costs one table build and a clean and invalidate of the 2 MiB output lease, 32,768 lines at 20 cycles per line, 0.33 ms on an A76 at 2,002 MHz. Board prediction for the eight-job session through the queue: 80 to 83 µs kick-to-timeline per job, 113 µs for the first, at most 0.5 µs added CPU time per job on an A76, measured on the 24 MHz counter as kick-to-timeline, submit-to-kick and timeline-to-record. Budgets: submit to kick 1 worker step and no tick wait; client wake-ups per job 1 record; worker wake-ups per job beyond interrupts 1; queue round trips 0; copies per byte 0; at most 57 transport and 6 maintenance DSB SY; at most 27 translations; 23 uncached ring stores; hang detection job_us plus at most the 4 ms backup poll.
conclusion: Not yet run: the submit-path timing through the queue has not been measured on a board.
